3. Consider how to evolve a statistical classification rule that would classify an individual
into one of two populations on the basis of a set of measurements on the individual.
A summary of the steps follows:
Step 1: The first requirement is to define the vector of observable variables that will be used
in making the classification. Statistical criteria can be used to determine whether variables
are useful for classification purposes. For example, the sample means can be obtained for
the two populations, and the differences between the means relative to their standard devia-
tions can be checked to select variables having large relative mean differences. In addition,
one can also look at the correlation between the variables being considered and eliminate
those that are too highly correlated with variables already selected. The cost of measuring
the variable should also be compared with the additional classification power that the vari-
able provides. Variable selection requires good judgment and should be tested by actually
determining the operational effectiveness of the resulting classification rule.
Step 2: Once the set of variables is determined, their distribution should be checked to see
how close the joint distribution of the variable is to being a multivariate normal distribution.
The efficiency of our linear classification rule depends upon how good the normal assump-
tion is. If a significant lack of normality is apparent, or if the covariance matrices are not

covariance matrices and the coefficients are properly determined, the linear function

Step 4: Given the linear classification function, one must determine the coefficients by solv-

Step 5: The final step in developing the classification rule is to determine the classification
constant. We introduced three criteria for determining this constant.
Step 6: Finally, one should make an evaluation of the operational effectiveness of the result-
ing classification rule. The statistician does this by considering the probabilities of making
different types of errors and determining the expected loss if losses and prior probabilities
are available. Although we restricted ourselves to the two-population case, the approach
presented can be generalized by considering many populations. One approach to the mul-
tipopulation problem is to perform sequential classifications by first aggregating the pop-

two-population technique can then be used to obtain a rule for classifying an individual into
one of the super populations. Each super population is then broken down into two smaller
aggregates, another classification rule evolved, and a classification made. This is repeated
until the final classification rule places an individual into a single population. If one knows

30.1 i ntroduction
Sometimes, the restrictions (such as predictor variables being quantitative or the dependent
variable not being a linear function of the predictors) for using multiple linear regression
cannot be met. We will investigate how to handle categorical predictors, curvilinear regres-
sion, and transformations to apply when errors are not normally distributed or the variance
is not homogeneous. The chapter concludes with a discussion of the problem of outliers and
a list of common mistakes made in regression analyses.
30.2 v isual t ests for v erifying the r egression a ssumptions
In deriving the expressions for regression parameters, we assumed:
n The predictor variables are linearly related to the response variable.
n Each predictor variable is not a random variable and they are measured without
any error.
n The errors are statistically independent.
n The errors are normally distributed with 0 mean and a constant standard deviation.
If any of these assumptions are violated, the conclusions based on the regression are suspect.
Often these assumptions are tested visually, as explained in the following sections.
30.2.1 t est for linearity
Preparing a scatter diagram of Y versus each predictor variable X can be helpful. Each graph
should have a linear relationship. Any outlier points on a graph should have their value
rechecked, as they might be due to some measurement error. If the graph is nonlinear, then
a curvilinear regression should be used instead of a linear regression.

A plot of the residuals as a function of the observation number, where the numbers are given
in the order in which the observations were made, can be implemented. Any trend up or
down in such a graph indicates the presence of other factors, or side effects, that varied from
one experiment to the next and affected the response. Causes for these trends should be
identified.

Notice that there isn’t a foolproof test for independence. We can only look at each potential
type of dependence individually, as illustrated in the previous two cases. Dependence can be
illustrated, but independence cannot be easily proven.
30.2.3 t est for normally distributed errors
For this test, a scatter diagram of the z scores for the response variable versus the z scores for
the errors can be made. If the plot is approximately linear, then the assumption for normally
distributed errors is satisfied.
30.2.4 t est for homoscedasticity
Homoscedasticity simply ensures that there is a constant standard deviation of errors. A scat-
ter diagram of errors versus predicted response can be used for this test. If the spread in one
part of the graph seems significantly different than that in other parts, then homoscedasticity
is not present.
30.3 t he p roblem of Multicollinearity
Two lines are collinear if they have the same slope and same intercept. These two lines can
be represented in just one dimension rather than the two dimensions required for lines
that are not collinear. This means that two collinear lines are dependent, not independent.
Similarly, when two predictor variables are linearly dependent, they are called collinear.
The linear dependence between variables is measured by their correlation. Therefore, if the
correlation between two predictor variables is nonzero, they are collinear. The problem of
linear dependence among many predictor variables is called the problem of multicollinear-
ity. When multicollinearity is present, the regression analysis may generate contradictory
results.

it is essential that they not move exactly in unison through the experiment. The standard

There are many indicators of multicollinearity. The correlation matrix for the regression
analysis can be investigated. Also, the problem is present if a set of predictors as a group
influence the response variable, but individually the same predictors demonstrate little influ-
ence on the response variable.

Another related problem occurs if redundant or irrelevant predictor variables are
included in a model. If these unnecessary variables are correlated with the other predic-
tor variables, then the variance of the coefficient estimates for the important variables
will be increased. As a result, the overall efficiency of the coefficient estimates will be
reduced.
The methodology for performing a multilinear regression analysis given in Chapter 29, “Mul-
tiple Linear Regression: Case Study,” is not based upon investigation and interpretation of
the coefficients; rather, the method simply looks at drops in the predictive efficiency of the
reduced model from the full model. As a result, this methodology is not as concerned about
multicollinearity.
30.4 r idge r egression
When a researcher finds that the explanatory variables that he is working with are highly cor-
related with each other, he should use ridge regression if he insists on interpretation of the
beta coefficients’ values as indicators of relative predictive importance.
In theory, ridge regression enables the researcher to obtain such an estimate by minimizing
mean square error risk. In practice, the large number of criteria that the researcher must
consider makes it difficult to select a particular set of coefficients. Nonetheless, ridge regres-
sion provides a useful diagnostic to check for sign stability.

An outlier is any observation that is atypical of the remaining observations. Excluding an
outlier for the analysis may lead to a misleading conclusion if the outlier in fact represents
a correct observation of the system behavior. The easiest way to identify outliers is to look
at the scatter plot of the data. Any value significantly away from the remaining observations
should be investigated for possible experimental errors. Once the possibility of errors in the
experiment has been eliminated, the researcher may decide to include or exclude the sus-
pected outlier based on intuition. One alternative is to repeat the analysis with and without
the outlier and state the results separately. Another alternative is to divide the operating
region into two or more subregions and obtain a separate model for each subregion.

chunks.heading: 31.1 Introduction
chunks.content:
31.1 Introduction
Previously we developed the t-test to decide, using independent samples, whether the
means of two populations are equal. To compare the means of three or more populations,
we employ a technique that compares the variability of the values of the dependent variable
in several samples.
In linear regression, the total variability of the values of the dependent variable is shown to
be the sum of the variation associated with the independent variables and the unexplained
variation not associated with the predictors. This idea, examining the sources of the varia-
tion of the dependent variable, is at the heart of a technique that can be thought of as com-
paring the means of several populations or as regression when the predictors are nominal
rather than at least ratio. Variation in the values of the dependent variable is broken into
components attributed to the independent variables and other, unexplained variation. Ratios
of these variations, or sums of squared deviations, are used to make inferences about the
population means. For this reason, the technique is called analysis of variance, or ANOVA.

31.3 Introduction to ANOVA
We begin with the case, corresponding to simple linear regression, in which the value of the
dependent variable is influenced by a single qualitative predictor. This is called one-way
analysis of variance. The predictor is called a factor and its values, called levels or treatments,

divide the observed cases into several groups. The corresponding groups of values of the
dependent variable are then samples from several populations. The levels of the factor are
fixed if all possible levels are included in the collected data or if inferences are to be drawn
about only the observed values. If the observed levels of the factor are a sample from the
population of all possible levels and inferences are to be drawn over all levels, whether repre-
sented in the data or not, the levels are random. Consider, for example, drawing conclusions
about all possible fertilizing patterns for wheat based on a study involving four such patterns.
In our first example, the levels of the factor are fixed, since conclusions are to be drawn only
over the levels mentioned in the data.
